newsitem.title: FRANCE: Austria forges confident EMU path with debt issue.
newsitem.headline: Austria forges confident EMU path with debt issue.

text.p: Austrian plans to sell a French franc eurobond next week, which it will convert into euros in 1999, underlined its confidence in the process of monetary union and saved it money at the same time, anaylsts said on Friday.

Austria's move to make the franc bond exchangeable with an existing Austrian bond denominated in schillings may be the first in a series of issues by countries likely to join the euro in currencies other than their own, they said.

"Clearly it's another way for a government to demonstrate explicitly its determination, commitment and optimism in the process of monetary union," Iain Lindsay, senior bond analyst at Credit Lyonnais, said. "There's a strong political statement built into this - the train is picking up a little more speed as each day passes."
Lindsay expected an easy conversion into euros since the bonds have the same characteristics.
So when French francs and Austrian schillings disappear as planned on the introduction of a single currency in 1999 the bonds would effectively be the same.
A banker at one of the leads, said, "This clause has a very strong political side to it, which is important for Austria."
They also said they saw "fungibility of several issues of parallel bonds, denominated in different currencies of European monetary union...in a large euro issue."

Syndication managers said the 5.5-percent January, 18 2004 bond, the same terms as the schilling Bund already in existance, would probably be sold with a yield between five and seven basis points above French government bonds.
But with French yields currently 21 basis points below equivalent Austrian yields, the government would still be saving about 15 basis points on the cost of funding its deficit.
Analysts said if other countries were to follow Austria's lead, the French market could well be a popular choice given that its yields are among the lowest in Europe.

"There are not many reference curves under (Austria's) with secondary markets this tight, and if this kind of approach becomes more frequent, the French market will continue to be tapped," Lindsay said.
Part of the attraction of the issue, seen at three and five billion francs, was a built in guarantee of high liquidity when it and the schilling bond are converted into euros in 1999.
The ultimate aim is to have a "super liquid Austrian euro Bund or a super liquid euro Eurobond," said Joe Cook head of European capital markets at JP Morgan.
The outstanding amount of the schilling Bund, a benchmark in the domestic Austrian market, totaled some 15.46 billion schillings or 7.5 billion French francs.

The French government has already taken similar steps in its own bond market. It has two Ecu and French franc government bonds with the same coupon and maturity dates. It has said they will be fungible when they are both converted into euros.
"This promise of additional liquidity in times to come is giving the 10-yr Ecu bonds help as well," Lindsay said.

Some syndication managers in Paris said this feature of convertibility was little more than a "gimmick," saving money for Austria being the main objective. But they said it had still aroused a great deal of interest among investors and was the main topic of conversation in Paris on Friday.
